item.title: Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia
item.description: Indonesian stocks suffered a massive 11 per cent decline on Friday after MSCI threatened its "emerging market status", which could prompt massive foreign selloff from the Southeast Asian economy.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia

Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia Indonesian stocks suffered a massive 11 per cent decline on Friday after MSCI threatened its "emerging market status", which could prompt massive foreign selloff from the Southeast Asian economy.

Beyond the sell-off: What an MSCI downgrade threat could mean for Indonesia

Saloni Goel New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 1:54 PM IST

Listen to This Article

MSCI’s proposed downgrade of Indonesia is less about immediate passive outflows and more about the long-term cost of losing benchmark inclusion, according to analysts.   Indonesian stocks suffered a massive 11 per cent decline on Friday after MSCI threatened its "emerging market status", which could prompt massive foreign sell-off from the Southeast Asian economy.   According to a Reuters report, Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite plunged as much as 11.4 per cent to its lowest point since early November 2020, clocking its worst one-day drop since January 1998. Earlier in the day, the benchmark opened 8 per cent lower, which triggered a 30-minute trading halt.   MSCI reported that market participants had raised significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market, including persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behaviour.   The index aggregator is considering moving Indonesia from Emerging Market to Standalone status, with feedback until April 30, 2027 and a decision by June 30, 2027.   What does it mean for Indonesia?     Indonesia's weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets index fell from 1.16 per cent at the end of 2025 to 0.43 per cent by September 30, and its constituents fell from 18 to 9, as MSCI froze additions and deleted names flagged under Jakarta's own concentrated-holding framework, Harshal Dasani, business head at INVasset PMS, said. At 0.43 per cent, he said, that forced passive selling runs to a few billion dollars, which is less than the market lost in Friday's session.   For the year, the index is down 39 per cent, making it one of the worst-performing emerging markets this year.   ALSO READ:  Stock Market LIVE: Sensex gains 300 pts, Nifty tops 23,100; Nifty IT rises over 3%

Justin Khoo of VT Markets said that forced selling by index-tracking funds, potentially accelerating foreign outflows, weakening the rupiah, and tightening domestic financial conditions are the immediate concerns for the market.   "An 11% plunge alone is unlikely to destabilize Indonesia's financial system. However, with the country's stock market already down nearly 40% this year, sustained foreign capital outflows could weaken market liquidity, discourage investment and further erode investor confidence," he added.   Standalone status, according to Dasani, is the index equivalent of delisting from global portfolios. This would make foreign ownership a discretionary hedge-fund decision rather than an allocation, and the cost of equity rises for years. He observed that Argentina went standalone in 2021 over capital controls and is still there.   Limited global spillover   Despite being Southeast Asia's largest economy, Indonesia is a small part of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, suggesting limited direct global spillover.   Other ASEAN markets may benefit from portfolio reallocations, although broader regional sentiment remains vulnerable, he noted.   Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. Home / World News / Fed Chair Warsh stresses price stability, offers no signals on rate outlook

Fed Chair Warsh stresses price stability, offers no signals on rate outlook The US central bank raised its key rate by 25 basis points in September, defying US President Donald Trump's calls for cuts, as persistent inflation keeps further tightening on the table

US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh | Image: Bloomberg

AP Bangkok 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 1:37 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday he won't prejudge what the US central bank will do about interest rates at its upcoming meetings in October and December. The Fed increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years, and stubbornly elevated US inflation will likely lead it to hike that rate again in coming months to slow spending and help cool price pressures. But Warsh offered no fresh signals during a "fireside chat" with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok.

"At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," Warsh said. "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."   The Fed's September rate hike defied US President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates. The president criticised the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The global surge in prices is a key concern of central bankers and financial leaders meeting in Bangkok.

Also Read

Let exchange rate act as shock absorber: IMF on Fed hike impact on India

Fed, ECB minutes to show inflation fears as near-term rate hike bets fade

US Fed may skip October rate hike as labour market cools more than expected

Fed watchdog finds deficiencies but no misconduct in Powell-era project

Rupee settles 2 paise up at 95.89 against dollar after breaching 96 level

According to minutes released from the most recent meeting, most Fed officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year. That would raise borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans, and credit cards over time. Warsh said the surge in investment driven by the craze for artificial intelligence is one of the factors behind higher inflation and the Fed's task force on issues related to AI will meet Nov. 16. "I'd say the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the US and the global economy in my lifetime to this point," he said.

Unlike military conflict and other shocks that are driving prices higher, Warsh said he believes AI will bring "huge benefit" to the world economy in time. For Fed economists who struggle to foresee the future using data that lags behind today's realities, AI could prove a vital tool, he said. "We torture data with old fashioned models to try to find out what's underlying inflation trends. Not so long from now, it won't be torture. We will have access at the fingertips of central banks to all the information in the world, and we'll be able to use new analytical tools to distill that data," he said.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / How Spain's housing crisis sparked nationwide protests and a snap election

How Spain's housing crisis sparked nationwide protests and a snap election Spain's housing crisis has sparked protests over soaring rents, evictions and holiday rentals. PM Pedro Sanchez has called a snap election for November 29 after parliament rejected housing measures

Protesters want the government to treat housing as a basic need rather than an asset primarily used to generate profits. (Photo: Screengrab/Reuters)

Rimjhim Singh New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 1:12 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Spain’s worsening housing crisis has triggered protests across the country, putting Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez under pressure and turning affordable housing into a major issue ahead of the next general election.   Protests in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and Malaga have brought together tenants, housing activists and residents angry about rising rents, evictions and the difficulty of finding affordable homes. The attempted eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid became a symbol of the crisis.   The protests have added to pressure on Sanchez’s government, which has struggled to secure parliamentary support for emergency housing measures. Sanchez announced a snap general election for November 29, 2026, bringing the vote forward from 2027.

What are the protests about?   Protesters want the government to treat housing as a basic need rather than an asset primarily used to generate profits. Their demands include stronger protection for tenants, measures to prevent evictions and steps to bring rents within reach of ordinary households.   According to Reuters , Spain faces a housing shortage of about 750,000 homes, a figure that the Bank of Spain expects to rise to more than one million by 2028. Also Read

Can AI 'feel' pain? Anthropic bans 'cruel' behaviour towards its models

Can every citizen claim to be journalist? SC says issue needs 'examination'

Delhi property tax waiver extended to Dec 31: Claim process explained

US scraps 540-day work permit extension: What immigrant workers must know

The attempted eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old pensioner in Madrid, became a rallying point for the movement. Her case highlighted the difficulties faced by vulnerable residents who risk losing their homes in an increasingly expensive market. Fox News reported that her death on October 7 further intensified public anger.

Protesters have called for stronger tenant protections, limits on rent increases and action against property speculation. They also want the government to increase the supply of affordable housing and prevent evictions that leave vulnerable people without a home.   Tourism and property speculation add to the crisis   Mass tourism has become another source of tension, particularly in Barcelona, where residents blame the growth of holiday rentals for reducing the supply of homes available to permanent residents. Some property owners prefer short-term tourist rentals because they can be more profitable than long-term leases.   According to Fox News , Barcelona and the surrounding region received 26.1 million visitors in 2025, generating an estimated $15.4 billion in direct tourism spending.

Housing activists argue that the growth of short-term holiday rentals reduces the supply of homes available to permanent residents and puts upward pressure on rents. Research cited by the European Parliament has linked the concentration of short-term rentals in some Barcelona neighbourhoods to rising housing costs and the displacement of residents.   Tourism is not the only cause of the crisis. A shortage of homes, rising demand, property investment and the gap between wages and rents have all contributed. However, the growth of holiday rentals has made the conflict between visitors and residents more visible.   The Spanish government has proposed restricting corporate purchases of residential property as part of its efforts to curb speculation and address the housing shortage. However, the proposals have drawn criticism from property developers. Carolina Roca, president of the Association of Property Developers of Madrid, told Reuters that the legal uncertainty created by the decrees could slow investment in affordable housing.

What are protesters demanding?   Protesters want housing to be treated as a basic need rather than an asset primarily used to generate profits. Their demands include rent controls, stronger protection against evictions, restrictions on short-term rentals and more public and affordable housing.   The crisis has also drawn in Spain's trade unions. The country's two largest unions, the General Union of Workers (UGT) and the Workers' Commissions (CCOO), announced plans for a nationwide general strike on November 11, Reuters reported. The proposed strike is scheduled just over two weeks before the election.   Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants' Union, told Reuters : "We cannot ignore the fact that housing is where most of our wages go. What is the point of raising the minimum wage if housing costs are rising three, four or five times faster?"

Reuters reported that the average monthly rent of €1,176 was equivalent to about 98.7 per cent of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, citing the Youth Council of Spain. The figures show why housing has become a major concern for workers who may be employed but still struggle to afford a place to live.   Why did parliament reject Sanchez's housing measures?   Sanchez's government approved emergency housing measures on September 29. The proposals included extending protections against eviction for vulnerable tenants, limiting rent increases and regulating short-term and seasonal rentals.   According to the Spanish government's announcements, the package also included tax incentives for landlords offering affordable rents, interest-free loans of up to €50,000 for first-time homebuyers and funding to support social housing construction. The government proposed restricting purchases of residential property by investment funds accused of profiting from the shortage.

On October 2, parliament rejected the emergency housing package. The conservative People's Party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan separatist party Junts opposed the measures. Opposition parties argued that the proposals could create uncertainty for landlords and investors, discourage construction and reduce the supply of rental homes.   The government approved two housing decrees again on October 6, including measures to cap rent increases, temporarily restrict evictions and limit corporate purchases of residential property. Reuters reported that the rules would initially take effect through emergency legislation but would still require parliamentary approval. A separate proposal for the automatic renewal of rental contracts also needed support.

Sanchez defended the measures as necessary to protect tenants and tackle speculation. Reuters quoted him as saying they were "based on plain common sense". He also said the measures would "protect the most vulnerable".   Why did Sanchez call a snap election?   Sanchez announced on October 5 that Spain would hold a general election on November 29, bringing the vote forward from 2027.   The immediate trigger was the failure to secure parliamentary support for the government's housing measures.   A snap election is a vote held earlier than originally expected. In Spain, the prime minister can initiate an early election by requesting the dissolution of parliament under the constitutional process. The result will determine the composition of the national parliament, including the Congress of Deputies, which plays a central role in selecting the prime minister and approving legislation.

(With agency inputs)

Oil prices dip but head for weekly gains amid West Asia supply concerns The International Energy Agency agreed to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market and any oil remaining from a record release of emergency reserves pledged in March to boost supply

For this week so far, Brent has increased 0.72 per cent, while WTI has jumped 5.9 per cent

Reuters BEIJING 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 1:50 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Oil prices eased on Friday but were heading for weekly gains on uncertainty over Middle East supplies and a larger-than-expected draw from US crude stockpiles, while European diesel margins dropped following the IEA's decision to release more diesel.   Brent crude futures were down 47 cents, or 0.44 per cent, at $105.45 a barrel by 0747 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 62 cents, or 0.63 per cent, to $97.35.   WTI settled up more than 3 per cent on Thursday after a big US crude stock draw on hurricane production shut-ins.   For this week so far, Brent has increased 0.72 per cent, while WTI has jumped 5.9 per cent.

"Uncertainty in the Middle East and concerns over the sustainability of oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz has the market pricing in a significant risk premium," ING analysts wrote in a note. Also Read

West Asia war keeps $110 in sight for oil despite supply recovery: Analyst

Oil prices rise as traders weigh Saudi supply risk, Russian diesel flow

Oil volatility to rise ahead of midterm; Brent may test $120: Analyst

Record FPI outflows top ₹3 trillion in CY26, nearly double 2025 tally

Some kind of agreement between the US and Iran was required to provide more confidence to the market that stronger oil flows from the region would continue, they added. Iran says it is stepping up strikes near the Strait of Hormuz Supply jitters also increased as attacks around the Strait of Hormuz surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.

Total Hormuz clearance averaged 11.62 million barrels per day over the seven days to October 13, about 68 per cent of the 17.15 million bpd baseline, said ship tracking firm Kpler.   European diesel refining margins declined by nearly 2 per cent on Friday to $78.67 a barrel, after the International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market.   Those margins rose as high as $95 a barrel in September as diesel supply tightened because of wars in Ukraine and Iran.   "Intensified Iranian attacks drove Gulf crude flows sharply lower," Kpler analysts said in a report on Thursday, adding that they expected a slower and more uneven Hormuz recovery in the absence of a comprehensive political deal.

The Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing two guards, while the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen detailed dozens of attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the escalating conflict.   The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that have carried oil and petroleum products from countries such as Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in a bid to cut record global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.   The discussions come days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans.
